subject: armadillo
pitch: A nine-banded armadillo trotting along. A shell of overlapping banded plates in dusty pinkish-tan, a pointy snout, tall leathery ears, small beady eyes, sturdy clawed feet and a long armoured tail tapering to a point. A sprinkle of coarse pale hairs pokes out between the bands.
reasoning:
I'm sketching the armadillo's proportions, planning a body around 0.45m long with a shoulder height near 0.22m, a 0.15m head, and orienting the model to face +Z before placing primitives.

Now I'm defining materials for the shell, band seams, belly, snout, ears, eyes, claws and hair, then setting up the segmented shell using half-sphere domes scaled to the body shape with overlapping latitudinal bands to create the banded armor plates.

I'm reconsidering the approach: instead of slicing a sphere's latitude bands around the Y pole, which creates horizontal rings, I should build each band as a cylinder segment oriented along the body's length and rotate it into place along the Z axis.

Working out the rotation math for arc placement...

Actually, I realize a cleaner approach: rotate a sphere so its poles align with the Z axis, then latitude bands naturally form rings stacked along Z, which maps nicely onto the band structure I need.

This rotation approach is getting too fiddly, so I'm considering instead writing my own custom parametric dome function that builds cross-sections with elliptical profiles varying along the z-axis.

I'll shape the body profile so it tapers smoothly at both ends, then slice it into nine overlapping bands with slightly larger radii so they interlock naturally, letting the overhang create the segmented seam look without needing separate dark seam geometry.

For the shoulder and pelvic shields I'll just use scaled sphere caps placed at the front and back of the body. For the tail, instead of a constant-radius tube, I'll build it from a series of tapering cylindrical rings oriented along a curving path using lookAt-style rotation, so it narrows naturally toward the tip.

Then for the head I'm shaping a pointy snout from a rotated cone so the tip points forward, with leathery ears made from flattened, stretched spheres angled slightly back and positioned near the top of the head above the shell's front edge.

For the body, I'm adding a small head, tiny black eye spheres, a pinkish belly ellipsoid under the shell, and four tapered cylinder legs with flattened feet and small forward-pointing claws. I'm grouping each leg under a pivot so I can rotate them for a trotting gait, with diagonal pairs moving together, and scattering thin coarse hairs at the band seams, oriented outward along the shell's surface normal.

Setting up materials for the shell, belly, skin, eyes, claws, hairs, and tail bands, then starting the component code with a seeded random generator and defining the body's width and height profile along its length using a parabolic cross-section.

Still refining the band geometry, computing surface positions across angle and height with a shoulder bump and slight radial growth to avoid gaps between bands.

I should also set the material to double-sided in case normals get inverted from the winding order. For the tail, I'm planning 11 segments following a curved path that dips back and slightly upward, tapering the radius from the body toward the tip.

For the legs, I'm placing pivots near the belly with upper leg cylinders, flattened box feet, and small claw cones angled forward-down. I'm positioning the front and back legs at different z-offsets with diagonal pairs tilted for a trot pose.

Now I'm building the head group with a scaled sphere skull and a rotated cone snout, working out the positioning so the snout tip faces forward correctly.

I'm placing a tiny dark nose sphere at the snout tip, then positioning the ears as tilted, leathery-shaped spheres angled back from the head, before moving on to adding small black eye spheres.

Now I'm scattering fine hairs along the seams between shell bands—randomizing their position, angle, and tilt outward from the surface, giving them a thin cylindrical shape and pale cream coloring to poke out naturally between segments.

I'm also working out the belly geometry and leg placement so the model actually stands properly on the ground plane—adjusting the belly ellipsoid's position and radii, and figuring out pivot heights and leg lengths so the feet land at y=0 instead of sinking below the floor, loosely basing shell height proportions on a real nine-banded armadillo's dimensions.

Checking the trot rotation effect on foot height confirms the lift stays within tolerance, so I'll just accept the pose rotations as-is. Since the legs pivot at body-local y=0, which equals world BY, the feet land exactly at world y=0 — good, that settles the ground contact.

Now I'm working out claw placement: three small cones per foot, tilted downward and forward with a rotateX offset so the tips angle toward the ground, positioned slightly spread along the foot's front edge. For materials, I'm settling on a dusty tan/pink palette for the shell tones, lighter cream for hairs, a muted skin tone for legs and snout, near-black eyes, and pale claws.

I'm setting roughness values -- shells a bit glossy, hair matte -- and using flat shading for the low-poly look. Then I start writing the body-profile helper functions that compute width and height along the spine using falloff curves, followed by a band geometry generator that builds ring cross-sections stepping through the body length with adjustable growth and lip flare parameters.

Generating band geometry...

Thinking through band placement now: nine overlapping bands span the body length, each with a slight forward overlap and lip flare so one band's edge tucks under the next, mimicking a real armadillo's shell segments.

For the belly I'm adding a flattened, elongated sphere positioned slightly below center so it peeks out beneath the shell line while legs pass through it naturally. Then I'm working out where to scatter hair tufts along the seams by sampling random points on the shell's curved surface and computing surface normals so each tuft points outward correctly.

Now I'm turning to the tail, defining a curved path of positions tapering from a thick base near the shell down to a fine tip, building it from a series of frustum segments oriented along the path and alternating armor colors, with a small cone cap at the end.

Then I'm designing the head group: a scaled skull sphere, a conical snout rotated forward, a small dark nose, beady eye spheres placed on the skull's sides, and tall leathery ear shapes tilted backward at an angle. I'm starting to lay out the leg positions symmetrically around the body.

Still writing leg logic...

I'm now structuring the root group hierarchy, nesting the body, shell, legs, head, and tail together, and adding a slight downward head tilt for a more natural trotting pose. I'm also setting up material definitions and a seeded random number generator for procedural variation.

Now I'm building the tail as a series of tapering cylinder segments, computing position and radius along the curve so it narrows to a fine point at the tip, orienting each segment with quaternions to follow the tail's path.
